members: [Member 1] · question, context, method and attack lifecycle (slides 1 to 5)
[Member 2] · payload, affiliate model, victims and negotiation (slides 6 to 9)
[Member 3] · law enforcement, recommendations and conclusions (slides 10 to 12)

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Hi, I'm [Member 1], and this is our group's investigation of the RansomHub ransomware campaign. I'll take you through our question, the background, how we studied it and what one real attack looked like. [Member 2] will then cover the ransomware itself, the affiliate model, the victims and the negotiations, and [Member 3] will finish with law enforcement, our recommendations and our conclusions. Our headline is on the slide: RansomHub grew because its rivals were taken down, and it collapsed without the police ever touching it.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Our question has two halves. How did RansomHub's affiliates break in, extort their victims and negotiate? And did any law-enforcement action hurt the operation, or did the affiliates just move to another brand? To answer it we used one intrusion, logged in detail in November 2024, alongside eighteen public sources. The intrusion went through the Diamond Model and the kill chain, and each police action got a before-and-after comparison.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: RansomHub's timing matters. The FBI disrupted ALPHV in December 2023, and Operation Cronos hit LockBit in February 2024. RansomHub launched in between and picked up the affiliates those two groups left behind. By August 2024 the FBI and CISA had counted at least 210 victims, more than any other ransomware brand that year, and they put out a joint advisory. In April 2025 its servers went dark.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: To see how the affiliates worked day to day, we modelled one intrusion that The DFIR Report reconstructed from the victim's own logs. The attacker was an affiliate we can't name, working from a virtual machine. They used password spraying, Mimikatz, two remote-management tools and Rclone, and a handful of IP addresses for spraying, logging in and taking data. The victim had remote desktop open to the internet. We chose this case because every stage shows up in the logs. The two things we can't see are who the affiliate was and how much they demanded.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: For defenders, this timeline is the most useful thing we found. The password spray worked on day one, and the attacker went straight for the domain's credentials. On day two they scanned the network and put a remote-management tool on the backup servers. On day three they copied out just over two gigabytes. They came back through Splashtop on day five and encrypted on day six, 118 hours after first logging in. Every item on the right was a chance to stop them. Now [Member 2] will take you through the ransomware itself.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 2]. Before it encrypts anything, RansomHub's encryptor closes off every way back. It shuts down virtual machines and about thirty other processes, deletes the shadow copies and clears the event logs, and only then does it encrypt, with a separate key pair for each victim. It won't start without a password, it encrypts big files in chunks so it finishes quickly, and the operators even built their own tool, EDRKillShifter, to turn off security software first.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Affiliates joined for the money. They kept ninety percent of every ransom, paid straight into their own wallet. That mattered, because ALPHV had just walked off with a twenty-two million dollar payment that belonged to one of its own affiliates. The operators had rules, too: no targets in the former Soviet states, no hitting a victim again once it had paid, and from June 2024 a five-thousand-dollar deposit to join.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: By sector, the victim list looks random, and we think it is. Change Healthcare, Frontier, Christie's and Kawasaki Europe are in four different industries. What they had in common was exposure: remote desktop open to the internet, or an unpatched Citrix or Fortinet device on the edge of the network. Across those 210 victims the FBI counted eleven critical-infrastructure sectors. The one firm exclusion was geography.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: There's very little public negotiation data. Of 295 ransomware chats in the public archives, only one is RansomHub's, because each victim got a private chat that the affiliate ran. The incident-response firm Arete fills part of the gap: in its 2024 cases the median opening demand was nine hundred thousand dollars and the median payment three hundred and fifty thousand, so victims who paid settled at about thirty-nine percent. The public cases show the pressure. RansomHub claimed half a million Christie's clients, while Christie's notified about forty-six thousand, and both Kawasaki and Frontier were put on a countdown. Over to [Member 3].

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 3], and this table answers the second half of our question. The ALPHV and LockBit takedowns gave RansomHub its affiliates. The joint advisory published its tools, yet the November attack used exactly those tools. A Scattered Spider member, a known RansomHub affiliate, was charged in September 2025, after RansomHub had already gone dark. Nothing ever reached the people running it, and the affiliates moved on to DragonForce and Qilin. We should be clear about one limit: no one has confirmed why RansomHub collapsed, so a sealed investigation can't be ruled out.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: We have four recommendations, each tied to something we found. Watch the long middle of the attack: a burst of password guesses followed by a successful remote-desktop login, a machine that isn't a domain controller asking for domain credentials, and Rclone talking out on port 443. In a response, assume the data left before the encryption started, and check the attacker's claims against your own logs. Take remote desktop off the internet and keep edge devices patched. And keep offline backups, with a payment policy agreed before anyone needs it.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: To sum up, RansomHub was a brand wrapped around a mobile workforce of affiliates. The takedowns of its rivals built it, and market pressure ended it. Defenders get six days before encryption, and every one of those days left a trace. Because the same playbook now runs under DragonForce and Qilin, it pays to track the affiliates and how they work, whatever brand they happen to be using. We'd be glad to take your questions and feedback.
